accuracy.reason: All eight card objectives are accurate with scoped reverse-proxy example, L4/L7 distinction, policy signal limits, health sampling, state placement, drain limits, atomic retry safety and surviving capacity. Fail-open caveat matches AWS; diagrams make no migration guarantee.

evidence.quote: Check the product's all-unhealthy policy too. Some balancers send traffic to unhealthy targets when every target fails its checks, rather than refusing all traffic.

mechanisms.reason: Client/proxy/backend path and reusable connections explain routing; drain sequence and shared atomic operation record explain failures and safe repeats. Learner transfers these mechanisms to purchases.

evidence.quote: All backends use a shared durable database record of the key and result. In one transaction, insert a key that the database allows only once, create the note and record its result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without creating another note. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap.

coherence.reason: Notes request proceeds from routing to selection, failure detection, state, deployment and retries before whole-path capacity. Earlier connection distinction directly supports later drain reasoning.

evidence.quote: Stopping new L4 connections does not stop new HTTP requests on existing connections. A drain must also manage those connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests. L7 request-aware draining must still track already accepted work.

decisions.reason: Conditional algorithm selection uses duration and capacity, names hidden work and requires measurement. Costs, optional adoption, failure headroom and shared-database limits are explicit.

evidence.quote: For long, uneven work, consider least connections; for unequal server capacity, consider weights. Check actual latency and resource use before deciding: no policy is universally best.

clarity.reason: Backend, L4/L7, readiness, session state, affinity, in-flight, idempotency and headroom are explained with concrete examples. Neither diagrams nor text require unseen protocol details.

evidence.quote: Session state is information kept between a user's requests. If the Notes API keeps a user's session only in A's memory, B cannot read it. Losing A can lose the only copy.

outcomes.reason: C1: client/proxy/backend/response traced. C2: L7 paths and readable decrypted HTTP. C3: L4 connection reused for many requests. C4: distribution/redundancy versus adequate single server; slides 1/2 support all.

sourceChecks.claim: AWS ELB describes traffic distribution across backends; the scoped reverse-proxy diagram shows the backend doing work and response through proxy. Optional adoption is a workload decision.
Microsoft load-balancing options separates L4 transport from L7 path routing/TLS offload; connection reuse explains why L4 cannot independently choose each HTTP request.
NGINX defines round robin, least active connections and weighted traffic; configured signals do not measure arbitrary work or guarantee performance.
AWS target health documents periodic checks, failure thresholds and all-unhealthy fail-open; lesson correctly limits health-based guarantees.
Microsoft web-farm guidance requires shared state for cross-node access; local memory is independent. NGINX persistence does not replicate that state.

AWS deregistration stops new requests and gives a limited drain period; early termination may cause errors. Lesson correctly distinguishes existing connection reuse and does not claim unfinished work migrates.
AWS idempotent APIs requires stable request identity and atomic record/mutation to prevent crash gaps; retries with new IDs or node-only memory do not recognize a cross-node repeat.
Google SRE describes finite capacity despite load balancing and explicit overload rejection; redundant paths and surviving headroom are necessary, not availability guarantees.
